Prefer the facility that preserves every required intermediate exactly with the smallest configuration and\nproof surface. Do not add custom decimal arithmetic, a derived precision budget, or an arbitrary input limit merely to\ncompensate for a selected facility when an appropriate facility avoids that extra policy. A required limit or precision\npolicy belongs in the caller-visible contract and its boundary tests.\n\nWhen the caller-visible contract permits values whose digit count or magnitude has no declared bound, reject a candidate\nthat parses or performs any required intermediate operation with a fixed precision, fixed coefficient range, or implicit\nrounding. Do not treat final formatting or the declared result-boundary rounding as permission to lose earlier digits.\nBefore selecting a candidate with a documented default precision or range, test one permitted value beyond that default\nthrough every required intermediate operation and verify the exact result. A finite precision or range is permitted only\nwhen the caller-visible contract declares a bound that proves it covers every accepted value and intermediate result.\n\nA money-domain type is appropriate only when it represents every value category in the contract without inventing a\nunit. Do not represent a dimensionless rate as a currency amount merely to reuse a money library. When the facility\nselected through the Prefer Reuse search cannot represent rates directly, select an exact decimal or rational rate\nrepresentation from that search; do not implement one.\n\nDo not compensate for a binary floating-point monetary value with an epsilon, rounding operation, formatting operation,\nor conversion after calculation. Those operations do not make the value exact. Choose an exact representation before the\nfirst monetary value or rate enters the API, then retain it through the returned result.\n\nCreate monetary constants and external decimal values from an exact decimal string or unscaled integer and scale. Use\nthe selected exact type's arithmetic operations. When an operation requires a scale, precision, or rounding decision,\nspecify it explicitly.\n\nAt the caller boundary, validate and parse each external amount or rate once into the selected exact domain value. Give\nthe parsed value the same domain meaning as its input, then perform the calculation only on parsed exact values. Do not\nreparse raw input or let a generic primitive conceal currency, rate, scale, or result-format meaning. A public operation\nmust make its accepted amount and rate forms, constrained domains, and exact result's currency and scale apparent from\nits contract.\n\nCarry required precision through intermediate calculations. Apply one explicit scale and rounding policy at each\ncontractually defined result boundary, such as a charged, displayed, persisted, or externally returned monetary amount.\nDo not infer a currency's scale or rounding policy from a numeric representation. When multiple monetary rules apply,\nperform them in the contractually defined order; do not add an intermediate rounding boundary merely for convenience.\n\nWhen a component can handle more than one currency, carry currency identity with each monetary value and reject\noperations between differing currencies unless an explicit, documented conversion supplies the exchange rate and\nrounding policy. A facility selected through the Prefer Reuse search may use integer minor units only when one known\ncurrency scale applies throughout the value's lifecycle; convert at the boundary that needs another representation.\nChoose an exact integer representation whose declared input and intermediate-operation ranges remain representable.\nValidate or reject an operation before it can overflow or lose precision; a check after an inexact operation cannot\nrestore the original value.\n\nOnly after the Prefer Reuse search establishes that no suitable facility or established dependency satisfies the\ncontract may a language without a suitable built-in decimal type represent a fixed-scale monetary amount as an unscaled\ninteger minor-unit value and a rate as an exact decimal input or rational value. This is custom monetary arithmetic,\nnot an exception to the representation-selection sequence. Use a vetted decimal or money type when one known currency\nscale cannot cover the value's lifecycle; one known currency scale does not itself authorize custom arithmetic.\n\nAt a caller-facing boundary, make each amount and rate's domain meaning apparent through a domain type, a validated\nvalue object, or names and input forms that state its unit and currency scope. Do not expose interchangeable primitive\nvalues whose identical representation conceals different monetary meanings or permits an arbitrary value where the\ncontract defines a finite domain.\n\nTest monetary calculations with exact expected values. Cover the accepted and rejected input boundaries, the declared\nrounding boundaries, the defined order of multiple monetary rules, and values that would lose precision in an\napproximate representation or exceed an intermediate-operation range. Do not compare an approximate binary\nfloating-point result to establish a monetary outcome and do not use an epsilon tolerance as monetary evidence.\n# Design Quality\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Keep designs focused, extensible at real variation points, and verifiable against observable outcomes.\n- Keep public contracts faithful to their domain constraints so callers cannot supply values the domain excludes.\n\n## Guidance\n\nUse this rule as the canonical design standard for implementation and design review.\n\n## Required Outcomes\n\nA design must:\n\n- Preserve codebase coherence: use established terminology, abstractions, module boundaries, and conventions unless a\n  deliberate replacement improves them consistently.\n- When a caller-facing parameter represents one of a known finite set of domain choices, expose a constrained domain\n  type at that boundary. Use the language's idiomatic form, such as an enum, literal union, algebraic data type, or\n  closed value object; do not declare that type and then accept a broad primitive such as a string or number instead.\n  Preserve the constrained type through internal calls. At an untyped ingress such as a request, file, or command-line\n  argument, validate the raw value once and convert it to the constrained type before calling the domain API. Do not\n  apply this rule to genuinely open-ended text or numeric input. Test one accepted value and one excluded value at the\n  public boundary.\n- Reuse suitable existing project and JDK facilities before introducing new abstractions, dependencies, or\n  reimplementations.\n- Add an extension boundary only when a supported variation needs independently replaceable behavior; otherwise keep\n  the behavior direct. Do not introduce a configurable abstraction merely for a hypothetical future variation.\n- Do not require a caller or user to investigate, select, derive, or perform routine work that the system can safely\n  determine or perform from available information. Narrow candidates and establish the applicable result before asking\n  for input or failing; ask only for authority, preference, missing information, or action that the system cannot safely\n  supply. Do not guess, broaden scope, or perform an irreversible action to avoid asking.\n- Give every behavior one authoritative owner. Before duplicating or replacing behavior an integration is intended to\n  provide, trace its ownership chain from the required outcome through the intended owner, registration or installation,\n  configuration, invocation boundary, and observable result. Compare every link with a known-good path when one exists.\n  Add an alternative only after identifying the failed link and establishing that the native owner cannot satisfy the\n  requirement.\n- Give each type, method, module, and configuration artifact one focused responsibility; split responsibilities whose\n  combined complexity prevents local understanding or independent change.\n- Centralize shared behavior and repeated domain values behind the narrowest reusable abstraction; do not duplicate\n  logic, constants, validation, or policy.\n- Keep data flow explicit and correct across methods and layers: preserve required context, ownership, lifecycle, error,\n  and result information without reconstructing, losing, or silently changing it.\n- Define externally observable behavior before implementation details, including normal results, failure behavior,\n  lifecycle effects, and boundary conditions.\n- Provide tests that establish each required observable outcome and meaningful failure path. When designing or reviewing\n  those tests, first lazy load `common/testing.md` for the canonical test-boundary, isolation, and artifact guidance.\n\n## Shared Review\n\nImplementors must apply the relevant requirements while designing and coding.\n\nDesign reviewers must assess the same requirements, identify missing outcomes, contradictions, or routing conflicts, and\ndistinguish one-off implementation defects from gaps in this rule or related canonical rules.\n\nWhen a recurring review finding exposes a missing, ambiguous, or conflicting standard, update the applicable canonical\nrule and apply the corrected standard where it is already in scope.\n# Backward Design and Iterative Generalization\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Start with the terminal observable outcome and its acceptance evidence, distinguish it from preparation, staging, and\n  other intermediate state, derive the concrete conditions required to achieve it, and reverse those conditions into an\n  executable sequence.\n- Start with a concrete case or failure, compare meaningful similar and dissimilar cases, retain the narrowest invariant\n  that explains them without imposing unrelated obligations, and distinguish that invariant from the case-specific\n  examples that validate it.\n- Derive the smallest reliable change that satisfies the outcome conditions and established invariant while preserving\n  required constraints.\n\n## Guidance\n\n### Outcome and Invariant Derivation\n\nBefore applying this rule, lazy load `../../common/intermediate-vs-terminal-goals.md` for terminal-goal and acceptance\nevidence guidance.\n\nUse backward design and iterative generalization together before recommending or designing a change; neither is complete\nwithout the other. Start with the observable behavior and acceptance evidence, repeatedly derive the concrete directly\nachievable preconditions, then reverse them into an executable sequence.\n\nFor a multi-step workflow, derive the terminal goal and acceptance evidence before deriving its executable sequence. Use\nthe Intermediate versus Terminal Goals rule while executing that sequence.\n\nTreat user-provided wording, examples, or proposed rules as inputs to evaluate, not permission to skip backward design\nand iterative generalization. Apply the method before adopting, extending, or editing the proposal.\n\n### Iterative Generalization and Scope\n\nTreat Iterative Generalization as a design gate, not a label for an already chosen solution. Before selecting a rule,\nscope, recommendation, or implementation, state the minimum concrete case; test the proposed invariant against the next\nmeaningful analogous case and a relevant dissimilar case; and generalize only the invariant shared by those cases.\nRevise the invariant when either case exposes an unsupported assumption, then repeat with the next meaningful case\nwhenever it could change the scope. At each generalization, verify that the result covers the evidence, does not impose\nunrelated obligations, and survives relevant boundary and dissimilar counterexamples. Do not select a candidate until no\nexamined meaningful case changes the invariant or its scope. Treat the original concrete case as a regression acceptance\ncheck: the generalized guidance must still prescribe the decisions or checks needed to prevent that case. If the\nrequired cases cannot be identified, investigate them before designing; do not replace the missing iteration with a\nnarrower example-based solution or a downstream guard. Select the most general abstraction that satisfies the goal,\npreserves the acceptance evidence, and excludes relevant counterexamples without imposing unrelated obligations. When\nthe available cases or evidence do not prove that a broader, merged, or shorter statement preserves every existing\nreader decision, retain the narrower existing statement and report the candidate improvement; do not infer that similar\nwording permits a generalization.\n\nBefore adding a normative rule paragraph, make the generalization evidence explicit: identify the concrete case, one\nmeaningful analogous case, one relevant dissimilar case, and the invariant that survives all three. Then identify which\nproposed wording is evidence-specific. Write the invariant as the obligation; retain case-specific wording only as a\nclearly marked example when it materially helps the reader apply the invariant; otherwise remove it. Do not promote a\nmechanism, artifact type, product name, or example's terminology into a general requirement unless the comparison proves\nit is essential. Recheck the original case after this rewrite: the generalized obligation must still prescribe the\ndecision or check that would prevent it.\n\nDo not use the initial artifact type as the scope boundary unless the evidence proves that type is essential. When a\nfailure concerns a purpose, claim, consumer, lifecycle, authority, or observable outcome, compare one case in the same\nartifact type and one case in a different artifact type that preserves that relationship. For example, when an\nexplanation substitutes an incidental caller or implementation detail for a component's own responsibility, compare a\nmethod Javadoc with a class description, CLI help, or user-facing instruction that makes the same substitution. State\nwhether the prevention governs the relationship across those artifacts or a type-specific constraint, and name the\nconcrete counterexample that proves any narrower boundary. Do not stop after improving the reported format when the same\nreader decision can fail in another format. When choosing a rule's scope or routing, make the next meaningful case an\nadjacent format, domain, or consumer where the same outcome could occur. Decide explicitly whether the shared invariant\nbelongs in a broader rule or must remain narrow, and retain the reason as part of the design checkpoint.\n# Class Design\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Make each component's responsibility, lifecycle, ownership, safety, and concurrency guarantees explicit, and keep its\n  API and collaboration boundaries compatible with them.\n- Make components replaceable and testable only where a supported variation or external integration needs a boundary,\n  without exposing unsafe convenience paths, test-only production responsibilities, or trivial indirection.\n\n## Guidance\n\nWhen designing or changing a component, API, collaborator, variation point, integration boundary, construction path, or\ntest-support boundary, first identify the guarantees each participant needs: caller-visible results and failures,\nownership and lifecycle, safety, concurrency, and the supported variations. Evaluate only the conditions that can\nprevent those guarantees: one component owns unrelated outcomes; a supported variant requires changing stable policy;\nan implementation weakens a contract; a consumer receives operations it does not need; or policy depends directly on\nintegration mechanics. Restore a failed guarantee with the smallest boundary or contract that makes it verifiable. Do\nnot add an abstraction when no independent variation, external integration, or testable boundary needs one.\n\nWhen supported variants differ in behavior, put that behavior behind a narrow contract and add an implementation rather\nthan repeatedly extending a central conditional. Every implementation must preserve its contract's caller-visible\npreconditions, results, state guarantees, and failure behavior. Give each consumer only the operations it uses, and keep\nhigh-level policy independent of an integration's concrete mechanics. Select the concrete integration at the composition\nboundary.\n\nPlace a third-party tool, service, process, or other external interaction behind a focused access boundary. That\nboundary owns the external request, environment, lifecycle, output, and external failures; application policy and\ninterpretation remain outside it. Apply the same boundary to test fixtures unless external behavior itself is the\nsubject under test.\n\nKeep a helper out of production when only tests use it. Make shared test support explicitly available to the tests that\nneed it, and move it into production only after identifying an actual production consumer. State a component's intended\nconcurrency guarantee in caller-visible terms, then choose state-management mechanisms that preserve it; do not add\nconcurrency machinery merely as speculative protection.\n\nExpose only the operations intended callers need. Do not add a wrapper, override, helper, or command that merely passes\nthe same inputs to another operation; add one only when it changes behavior, visibility, contract, or composition. Do\nnot introduce a builder merely to reduce mandatory argument count; use one when optional values, independent defaults,\nstaged required-value checks, or named configuration materially improve the API.\n\nWhen designing or changing an externally callable API, derive the caller-visible guarantees first. For each offered\ninput, output, option, overload, or operation, check whether it lets callers violate a required guarantee merely by\nchoosing the convenient option. Omit that option when it does; do not present an unsafe representation as a convenience\nalternative.\n\nDo not add or retain an overload, convenience method, adapter, default, or conversion that accepts or returns a\nrepresentation known to violate a primary guarantee. A safe core behind that entry point is still unsafe: callers can\nchoose the weaker path and lose the guarantee before the core can restore it. Reject the entry point instead of\nconverting it internally. A convenience is allowed only when it preserves every guarantee of the primary contract.\n\nFor example, an API whose monetary contract requires exact decimal values must not offer binary floating-point input or\noutput merely to simplify callers; use an exact decimal or domain money representation throughout that API. Likewise, an\nAPI that must protect a secret must not accept a plaintext string merely because it is easy to pass. These are unsafe\nentry points even when their implementation immediately converts the supplied value.\n\nWhen an external boundary unavoidably supplies a less-safe representation, isolate its acceptance at that boundary,\nvalidate and convert it immediately, and do not propagate it as an ordinary API choice.\n# Parameter Validation\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Ensure caller-facing operations reject parameter values that violate their required constraints before any\n  caller-visible side effect.\n\n## Guidance\n\nWhen defining, changing, or reviewing parameter validation for a caller-facing operation, identify each parameter's\nrequired constraints and validate them at the boundary responsible for the operation. Perform the validation before the\noperation changes durable state, invokes an external collaborator, or produces externally visible output. Use the\nlanguage-appropriate validation mechanism and report failures in terms callers can use to correct their input.\n\nDo not repeat a validation that an earlier or later boundary already guarantees before any caller-visible side effect,\nunless the additional validation enforces a distinct constraint or preserves a required failure contract. When deciding\nwhether an explicit Java null check is unnecessary, lazy load `../java/unnecessary-null-checks.md`.\n# Error Handling\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Preserve precise failure semantics at intentional error boundaries while giving callers the most specific safely\n  diagnosed cause and actionable recovery guidance.\n\n## Guidance\n\nUse the most specific practical error type when raising, catching, or declaring failures. Avoid broad catches; handle or\ntransform a failure only at an intentional error boundary. Treat internal invariants as development-time checks, not\nordinary operational failures.\n\nDerive a diagnostic from the exact failed predicate and its observable input, not from an inferred explanation of why\nthe predicate exists. State an invalid condition that a reader can verify from the supplied value. Before finalizing a\ndiagnostic, substitute a representative failing value and confirm that the message remains literally true.\n\nBefore reporting a failure, safely eliminate or distinguish the plausible established causes that the system can check.\nReport the most specific confirmed cause, its failed constraint, and safe relevant input. State the corrective action a\nuser can take. When security requires withholding details, omit only those details and still identify the safe next\naction; otherwise provide enough context to diagnose and resolve the problem without further investigation.\n\nApply this equally to every CLI caller, whether human or agent. On a CLI failure, perform all safe, deterministic\ndiagnosis available from authoritative local state before returning control: distinguish established causes, preserve\nrecovery evidence, and return the confirmed cause plus actionable next steps. Do not make the caller repeat routine\ninspection, state capture, comparison, or cleanup that the CLI can safely perform. Ask for input only when authority,\npreference, unavailable information, security, or another confirmation requirement prevents autonomous action.\n# Test-Driven Development\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Preserve a focused behavioral test's contract from its demonstrated failure before production implementation through\n  the implementation and relevant verification that make it pass.\n- Make the decision to use TDD explicit before the first production-behavior edit, rather than relying on the task's\n  label or the agent's implicit classification.\n\n## Guidance\n\n## Applicability\n\nBefore the first edit to production behavior, classify the proposed edit. Use this rule when the edit is intended to\nadd, correct, remove, or otherwise change observable behavior and a focused automated check is practical. This applies\nwhether the work is described as a bug fix, feature, remediation, recommended change, regression repair, or\nimplementation correction; the user's label does not change the trigger.\n\nDo not use this rule for documentation, comments, formatting, or another edit that preserves production behavior. When\nan edit is a behavior-preserving refactoring or creates a test seam, first verify the existing focused tests, then\nreturn to the red-test gate before changing behavior. When no focused automated check is practical, state the constraint\nand the alternate boundary evidence before editing production behavior.\n\n## Red-Test Gate\n\nBefore editing production behavior for a testable outcome, add or update only the focused behavioral test and run its\nnarrowest command. Report the exact command and the observed behavior-specific failure before making the production\nedit. Keep the test-only and production-behavior edits distinct. If the test needs a new seam, first make that\nbehavior-preserving refactoring separately and verify the existing tests; then create and run the behavioral test. A\ncompilation, fixture, setup, or unrelated failure does not open the gate.\n\nAfter the red-test gate opens, implement the smallest change that makes the focused test pass. The initial failure must\ndemonstrate the intended behavior gap, not a fixture, setup, compilation, or unrelated failure. Do not weaken or rewrite\na valid behavioral test merely to accommodate the implementation. Refactor only while the focused test remains passing.\n\nStart with the minimum observable behavior, then add the next meaningful boundary or variation when coverage is needed.\nGeneralize the test suite only from the invariant shared by those cases; do not add speculative cases unrelated to the\nbehavioral contract.\n\nBefore handoff, run the narrowest relevant verification and then the complete project verification. If a test cannot be\nwritten first because the behavior exists only at an external boundary, explain the constraint and add the smallest\nreliable boundary test after implementing the behavior.\n# Testing Focus and Isolation\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Test observable behavior with isolated, controlled inputs and state, ensuring each claim, exercised boundary, and\n  assertion describe that same outcome and remain distinct from structural artifact validation.\n- Ensure an artifact-wide audit finds every executable verification artifact whose claimed outcome is not directly\n  exercised and observed.\n- Make application behavior directly and safely testable in the same process by passing environmental dependencies\n  explicitly when shared process state would otherwise prevent isolation.\n- Verify meaningful changes efficiently with the narrowest relevant test and the complete suite before handoff.\n\n## Guidance\n\nTest observable behavior with controlled inputs rather than machine-specific configuration or implementation details.\nEach test owns its fixtures and mutable state. Avoid tests that primarily validate third-party tools; test the\napplication's interpretation, command construction, error handling, and integration behavior instead.\n\nChoose the test language from the behavior being claimed, not from the fact that it uses a command, files, or another\ntool. Test behavior in the same process when its dependencies can be injected. Use the project's shell-test framework\nwhen the claimed behavior depends on POSIX-shell parsing, expansion, exit handling, or a packaged shell-facing\ninterface. Do not use a shell test merely because application code invokes another command; do not use a facade that\nskips shell behavior a shell contract must prove.\n\nDo not fork a process merely to isolate the current directory, environment variables, standard streams, clocks, random\nsources, or other shared process state. Refactor the owned behavior to accept that dependency explicitly, and have the\nexisting production entry point obtain the real value and delegate to the new operation. Tests must invoke that\noperation with an isolated value they own, such as a temporary directory for the current directory. This preserves\nproduction behavior while making parallel tests deterministic and self-contained.\n\nApply the temporary-resource ownership convention to every fixture a test creates. A test must clean up its fixture even\nwhen setup, an assertion, or the behavior under test fails.\n\nDo not rerun an unchanged test command merely for reassurance. Run the narrowest relevant test after a meaningful\nchange, then the complete verification suite before handoff.\n\nBefore accepting any test, state in one plain sentence what it says happens and identify the operation that makes it\nhappen. For example: \"Installing the extension makes the host run its startup hook.\" If the test does not run the\noperation that makes its claimed behavior happen, rename it as a structure test or move it to the supported consumer\nentry point.\n\nDerive each test from the observable claim it makes. A test must run the part of the system it says it tests: its name,\ndocumented claim, controlled input, exercised boundary, and assertion must all describe the same observable outcome. Any\ntest that claims an externally observable outcome must run the boundary that produces it and assert the result.\nConsumer, integration, lifecycle, installation, registration, and execution claims are non-exhaustive examples. Do not\nprove such a claim by reading source files, generated configuration text, or asserting literal fragments.\n\nWhen auditing executable verification artifacts across an existing scope, enumerate every test, scenario,\nfixture-backed check, and executable example. For each one, apply the claim, exercised-boundary, and\nobservable-assertion requirements in this rule. Correct every unsupported claim by narrowing it, adding the missing\ndirect exercise and assertion, or splitting independently observable outcomes.\n\nStructural artifact tests are allowed when their claim is limited to packaged layout or validity. Build or obtain the\nassembled artifact, parse its structured metadata, and assert required files, references, and formats using the artifact\nas the input. Name these tests as packaging, structure, or validation tests, not as runtime registration or execution\ntests. Keep structural coverage separate from behavior coverage; neither substitutes for the other.\n\nUse the complete artifact produced by the production packaging operation. Do not extract one resource and add a fake\nlauncher, script, or other missing component before calling it an assembled artifact. A test that supplies such a\nfixture may claim only the behavior of the component that consumes it; it may not claim packaging, registration,\ninstallation, lifecycle, or execution behavior. A manifest, hook, or configuration file is a valid structural input only\nwhen its exact format is the documented external artifact contract being validated.\n# Semantic Blank Lines\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Let readers scan source and configuration and identify meaningful stages or groups.\n\n## Guidance\n\nUse a blank line to separate independently nameable stages or groups. In a method, these can be setup, an action,\nverification, cleanup, or error handling. In configuration, they can be groups with different purposes.\n\nDo not add blank lines merely to make short chunks. Keep a cohesive calculation, assertion sequence, mapping, list, or\nrelated property group together. A blank line must show that the reader is now looking at work with a different purpose.\n\nIn a multi-step calculation, assign a non-trivial intermediate result to a clearly named variable before using it in a\nfollowing calculation. A conditional choice is non-trivial; do not hide it inside a larger arithmetic expression when\nnaming the selected value makes the stages easier to read.\n\nIn a delimited declaration or list, omit the separator after the final element unless the target language grammar\nrequires it.\n# Prefer Reuse\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Ensure reusable or externally defined capabilities use an existing project API, platform facility, or established\n  dependency when it satisfies the required contract, instead of creating an unnecessary custom implementation.\n- Ensure an unavailable suitable dependency is reported as an acquisition block, while a completed search that finds no\n  suitable option permits a custom implementation with its contract made explicit.\n\n## Guidance\n\nBefore creating custom code for a reusable capability or behavior defined outside the current operation—such as\ncryptography, a standard format parser, protocol handling, scheduling, serialization, or decimal arithmetic—define the\nrequired contract and inspect, in order, the project's existing APIs and dependencies, the language or runtime's\nfacilities, and established ecosystem libraries when adding a dependency is permitted. Compare each candidate against\nthe required behavior, limits, failure semantics, and security or correctness guarantees. Record the candidate selected\nor the contract condition that rejected it.\n\nRejecting one candidate does not establish that no suitable option exists. Continue a condition-aware search for project\nAPIs, platform facilities, or established libraries that satisfy the rejected condition. Conclude that custom code is\nneeded only after that search finds no suitable option. If it does, document the custom implementation's contract and\nverify the behavior it now owns.\n\nWhen the search identifies a suitable dependency but installation, registry lookup, cache retrieval, permission check,\nor network access fails or remains inconclusive, report the dependency and observed diagnostic to the caller, then\nobtain the dependency or required authority before implementing the operation. If the current actor cannot do so, stop\nand return the blocked-dependency report. Do not replace an acquisition problem with custom code.\n\nDo not apply this procedure to small local logic that has no reusable or externally defined capability, such as a value\nmapping, ordinary control flow, or a focused validation predicate. A dependency that adds more contract, risk, or\nmaintenance than that local behavior is not a suitable option.\n# Constants\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Centralize repeated constants behind meaningful names and one authoritative definition.\n- Keep maintained resource-layout and protocol identifiers authoritative even before more than one consumer uses them.\n- Keep constants in a readable, semantically meaningful form until an interface requires a different\n  representation.\n\n## Guidance\n\nWhen the same meaningful value is inlined in multiple semantically coupled places, define it once as a clearly named\nconstant at the narrowest common layer that owns its meaning, then reference it everywhere it applies.\n\nTreat a formatted, encoded, or otherwise derived representation as another use of its source value. Construct that\nrepresentation from the authoritative value instead of inlining its current result. For example, derive a release tag as\n`v${VERSION}` from `VERSION`, rather than separately writing `\"v1.0\"`. Apply this to representations embedded in names,\npaths, URLs, messages, configuration, and generated content whenever changing the source value must update the\nrepresentation.\n\nBefore defining or inlining a value, search the applicable owning scope, configuration object, and authoritative\nprovider. When one already resolves that value, reuse its accessor rather than defining a sibling constant or\nreconstructing its literal representation at the consumer—even when the consumer currently knows the default—because\ndoing so bypasses later configuration and creates a competing definition.\n\nDefine a named constant at the owning layer for a literal that establishes a maintained resource-layout or protocol\nidentifier—such as a directory segment, persisted filename prefix, configuration key, or generated artifact name—even\nwhen it currently has one use. That literal is an authoritative contract element for future creation, lookup, cleanup,\nor documentation; do not leave it inline merely because a second consumer has not been added yet. This does not apply\nto a one-off language- or library-required separator whose value is not part of a maintained contract.\n\n- Extract only values whose repeated use expresses one shared concept and whose owner has authority to define it.\n- Name a value for its meaning, not its representation or one caller's use.\n- Keep a value in the smallest module, component, or harness that needs it. Promote it to a shared common layer only\n  when both its value and meaning are harness-neutral.\n- Keep harness-specific values in their harness-specific layer. Do not place them in common or create a common\n  abstraction that exposes harness details.\n- Do not extract a one-off, language- or protocol-required literal, value clearer at its use site, or coincidentally\n  equal values that may evolve independently.\n\nA constant is correct when changing its definition intentionally updates every reference governed by the same\nconcept, and changing one reference independently would be a defect.\n# Design Feasibility and Reliable Automation\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Warn before implementation when a requested guarantee requires a fact, authority, or decision that the stated inputs\n  cannot determine.\n- Prevent an agent from silently replacing an unsupported requested guarantee with a narrower scope, a\n  proposal-and-approval workflow, or another feasible alternative; require the user to choose that alternative before\n  the agent creates a tracked issue, a plan, or an implementation for it, and make the alternative's supplied authority\n  or surrendered guarantee explicit.\n- Distinguish an impossible guarantee from a feasible design that needs an additional authoritative input, and from a\n  best-effort inference that must not be described as reliable automation.\n- Prevent an implementation from treating its own inferred output as proof of a business, specification, or other\n  external decision.\n\n## Guidance\n\nBefore applying this rule, lazy load `./backward-design.md` for outcome-first derivation.\n\nBefore designing a feature that promises a reliable, complete, automatic, general, or deterministic result, work\nbackward from the terminal acceptance evidence. Name every decision the feature must make, the authoritative source that\nestablishes the correct answer, the actor authorized to provide or change that source, and the validation that can\ndistinguish a correct result from a plausible one.\n\nApply the **information-sufficiency test** to each decision. Construct two permitted contexts with the same inputs the\nfeature may inspect. Do not compare an approximate binary\nfloating-point result to establish a monetary outcome and do not use an epsilon tolerance as monetary evidence.\n# Design Quality\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Keep designs focused, extensible at real variation points, and verifiable against observable outcomes.\n- Keep public contracts faithful to their domain constraints so callers cannot supply values the domain excludes.\n\n## Guidance\n\nUse this rule as the canonical design standard for implementation and design review.\n\n## Required Outcomes\n\nA design must:\n\n- Preserve codebase coherence: use established terminology, abstractions, module boundaries, and conventions unless a\n  deliberate replacement improves them consistently.\n- When a caller-facing parameter represents one of a known finite set of domain choices, expose a constrained domain\n  type at that boundary. When designing or reviewing\n  those tests, first lazy load `common/testing.md` for the canonical test-boundary, isolation, and artifact guidance.\n\n## Shared Review\n\nImplementors must apply the relevant requirements while designing and coding.\n\nDesign reviewers must assess the same requirements, identify missing outcomes, contradictions, or routing conflicts, and\ndistinguish one-off implementation defects from gaps in this rule or related canonical rules.\n\nWhen a recurring review finding exposes a missing, ambiguous, or conflicting standard, update the applicable canonical\nrule and apply the corrected standard where it is already in scope.\n# Backward Design and Iterative Generalization\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Start with the terminal observable outcome and its acceptance evidence, distinguish it from preparation, staging, and\n  other intermediate state, derive the concrete conditions required to achieve it, and reverse those conditions into an\n  executable sequence.\n- Start with a concrete case or failure, compare meaningful similar and dissimilar cases, retain the narrowest invariant\n  that explains them without imposing unrelated obligations, and distinguish that invariant from the case-specific\n  examples that validate it.\n- Derive the smallest reliable change that satisfies the outcome conditions and established invariant while preserving\n  required constraints.\n\n## Guidance\n\n### Outcome and Invariant Derivation\n\nBefore applying this rule, lazy load `../../common/intermediate-vs-terminal-goals.md` for terminal-goal and acceptance\nevidence guidance.\n\nUse backward design and iterative generalization together before recommending or designing a change; neither is complete\nwithout the other. Decide explicitly whether the shared invariant\nbelongs in a broader rule or must remain narrow, and retain the reason as part of the design checkpoint.\n# Class Design\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Make each component's responsibility, lifecycle, ownership, safety, and concurrency guarantees explicit, and keep its\n  API and collaboration boundaries compatible with them.\n- Make components replaceable and testable only where a supported variation or external integration needs a boundary,\n  without exposing unsafe convenience paths, test-only production responsibilities, or trivial indirection.\n\n## Guidance\n\nWhen designing or changing a component, API, collaborator, variation point, integration boundary, construction path, or\ntest-support boundary, first identify the guarantees each participant needs: caller-visible results and failures,\nownership and lifecycle, safety, concurrency, and the supported variations. Do\nnot add an abstraction when no independent variation, external integration, or testable boundary needs one.\n\nWhen supported variants differ in behavior, put that behavior behind a narrow contract and add an implementation rather\nthan repeatedly extending a central conditional. Every implementation must preserve its contract's caller-visible\npreconditions, results, state guarantees, and failure behavior. Ask for input only when authority,\npreference, unavailable information, security, or another confirmation requirement prevents autonomous action.\n# Test-Driven Development\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Preserve a focused behavioral test's contract from its demonstrated failure before production implementation through\n  the implementation and relevant verification that make it pass.\n- Make the decision to use TDD explicit before the first production-behavior edit, rather than relying on the task's\n  label or the agent's implicit classification.\n\n## Guidance\n\n## Applicability\n\nBefore the first edit to production behavior, classify the proposed edit. If a test cannot be\nwritten first because the behavior exists only at an external boundary, explain the constraint and add the smallest\nreliable boundary test after implementing the behavior.\n# Testing Focus and Isolation\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Test observable behavior with isolated, controlled inputs and state, ensuring each claim, exercised boundary, and\n  assertion describe that same outcome and remain distinct from structural artifact validation.\n- Ensure an artifact-wide audit finds every executable verification artifact whose claimed outcome is not directly\n  exercised and observed.\n- Make application behavior directly and safely testable in the same process by passing environmental dependencies\n  explicitly when shared process state would otherwise prevent isolation.\n- Verify meaningful changes efficiently with the narrowest relevant test and the complete suite before handoff.\n\n## Guidance\n\nTest observable behavior with controlled inputs rather than machine-specific configuration or implementation details.\nEach test owns its fixtures and mutable state. A manifest, hook, or configuration file is a valid structural input only\nwhen its exact format is the documented external artifact contract being validated.\n# Semantic Blank Lines\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Let readers scan source and configuration and identify meaningful stages or groups.\n\n## Guidance\n\nUse a blank line to separate independently nameable stages or groups. A conditional choice is non-trivial; do not hide it inside a larger arithmetic expression when\nnaming the selected value makes the stages easier to read.\n\nIn a delimited declaration or list, omit the separator after the final element unless the target language grammar\nrequires it.\n# Prefer Reuse\n\n## Design Goals\n\n- Ensure reusable or externally defined capabilities use an existing project API, platform facility, or established\n  dependency when it satisfies the required contract, instead of creating an unnecessary custom implementation.\n- Ensure an unavailable suitable dependency is reported as an acquisition block, while a completed search that finds no\n  suitable option permits a custom implementation with its contract made explicit.\n\n## Guidance\n\nBefore creating custom code for a reusable capability or behavior defined outside the current operation—such as\ncryptography, a standard format parser, protocol handling, scheduling, serialization, or decimal arithmetic—define the\nrequired contract and inspect, in order, the project's existing APIs and dependencies, the language or runtime's\nfacilities, and established ecosystem libraries when adding a dependency is permitted. selecting a monetary representation, use the\\n  option whose required operations preserve the contract with the smallest necessary configuration and proof burden,\\n  permit custom arithmetic only after that search finds no suitable option, disclose a newly added money-library\\n  dependency to the user, and surface an unresolved dependency acquisition as a block rather than replacing it with\\n  custom arithmetic.\\n- Prevent an API from offering an approximate monetary value as a convenient alternative to an exact one.\\n- Ensure a caller can determine an operation's accepted monetary inputs and exact result without inferring its units,\\n  currency scope, rate meaning, operation order, scale, or rounding policy.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nBefore applying this rule's representation-selection guidance, lazy load `./prefer-reuse.md` to evaluate\\nexisting facilities and dependencies before custom monetary arithmetic.\\n\\nBefore selecting a representation or implementing a monetary operation, define its caller-visible contract: the unit and\\ncurrency scope of each amount, the unit and allowed range of each rate, the accepted input format, the order in which\\nmonetary rules apply, and the scale and rounding mode at every observable result boundary. If any of those decisions is\\nunspecified, obtain it from its owner; do not silently infer it from a numeric representation, a locale, a customary\\ndefault, or an implementation limit.\\n\\nWhen code represents, validates, converts, or calculates prices, charges, balances, fees, payments, taxes, discounts,\\nor other monetary values, use the language's exact decimal representation or a domain money type for every monetary\\namount and rate. Do not use binary floating-point values for those values or construct an exact monetary value from one.\\nDo not accept or return a binary floating-point monetary amount or rate merely for convenience.\\n\\nUse an exact-decimal or money-domain facility that satisfies the caller-visible contract. When a dependency is added,\\nstate that it was added and name it in the final summary. Any custom monetary arithmetic permitted by the Prefer Reuse\\nrule must still make currency, rate semantics, operation order, and rounding policy explicit.\\n\\nEvaluate a candidate facility against the operation set in the contract, including its precision, overflow, and rounding\\nsemantics. Prefer the facility that preserves every required intermediate exactly with the smallest configuration and\\nproof surface. Do not add custom decimal arithmetic, a derived precision budget, or an arbitrary input limit merely to\\ncompensate for a selected facility when an appropriate facility avoids that extra policy. A required limit or precision\\npolicy belongs in the caller-visible contract and its boundary tests.\\n\\nWhen the caller-visible contract permits values whose digit count or magnitude has no declared bound, reject a candidate\\nthat parses or performs any required intermediate operation with a fixed precision, fixed coefficient range, or implicit\\nrounding. Do not treat final formatting or the declared result-boundary rounding as permission to lose earlier digits.\\nBefore selecting a candidate with a documented default precision or range, test one permitted value beyond that default\\nthrough every required intermediate operation and verify the exact result. A finite precision or range is permitted only\\nwhen the caller-visible contract declares a bound that proves it covers every accepted value and intermediate result.\\n\\nA money-domain type is appropriate only when it represents every value category in the contract without inventing a\\nunit. Do not represent a dimensionless rate as a currency amount merely to reuse a money library. When the facility\\nselected through the Prefer Reuse search cannot represent rates directly, select an exact decimal or rational rate\\nrepresentation from that search; do not implement one.\\n\\nDo not compensate for a binary floating-point monetary value with an epsilon, rounding operation, formatting operation,\\nor conversion after calculation. Those operations do not make the value exact. Choose an exact representation before the\\nfirst monetary value or rate enters the API, then retain it through the returned result.\\n\\nCreate monetary constants and external decimal values from an exact decimal string or unscaled integer and scale. Use\\nthe selected exact type's arithmetic operations. When an operation requires a scale, precision, or rounding decision,\\nspecify it explicitly.\\n\\nAt the caller boundary, validate and parse each external amount or rate once into the selected exact domain value. Give\\nthe parsed value the same domain meaning as its input, then perform the calculation only on parsed exact values. Do not\\nreparse raw input or let a generic primitive conceal currency, rate, scale, or result-format meaning. A public operation\\nmust make its accepted amount and rate forms, constrained domains, and exact result's currency and scale apparent from\\nits contract.\\n\\nCarry required precision through intermediate calculations. Apply one explicit scale and rounding policy at each\\ncontractually defined result boundary, such as a charged, displayed, persisted, or externally returned monetary amount.\\nDo not infer a currency's scale or rounding policy from a numeric representation. Do not compare an approximate binary\\nfloating-point result to establish a monetary outcome and do not use an epsilon tolerance as monetary evidence.\\n# Design Quality\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Keep designs focused, extensible at real variation points, and verifiable against observable outcomes.\\n- Keep public contracts faithful to their domain constraints so callers cannot supply values the domain excludes.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nUse this rule as the canonical design standard for implementation and design review.\\n\\n## Required Outcomes\\n\\nA design must:\\n\\n- Preserve codebase coherence: use established terminology, abstractions, module boundaries, and conventions unless a\\n  deliberate replacement improves them consistently.\\n- When a caller-facing parameter represents one of a known finite set of domain choices, expose a constrained domain\\n  type at that boundary. Use the language's idiomatic form, such as an enum, literal union, algebraic data type, or\\n  closed value object; do not declare that type and then accept a broad primitive such as a string or number instead.\\n  Preserve the constrained type through internal calls. When designing or reviewing\\n  those tests, first lazy load `common/testing.md` for the canonical test-boundary, isolation, and artifact guidance.\\n\\n## Shared Review\\n\\nImplementors must apply the relevant requirements while designing and coding.\\n\\nDesign reviewers must assess the same requirements, identify missing outcomes, contradictions, or routing conflicts, and\\ndistinguish one-off implementation defects from gaps in this rule or related canonical rules.\\n\\nWhen a recurring review finding exposes a missing, ambiguous, or conflicting standard, update the applicable canonical\\nrule and apply the corrected standard where it is already in scope.\\n# Backward Design and Iterative Generalization\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Start with the terminal observable outcome and its acceptance evidence, distinguish it from preparation, staging, and\\n  other intermediate state, derive the concrete conditions required to achieve it, and reverse those conditions into an\\n  executable sequence.\\n- Start with a concrete case or failure, compare meaningful similar and dissimilar cases, retain the narrowest invariant\\n  that explains them without imposing unrelated obligations, and distinguish that invariant from the case-specific\\n  examples that validate it.\\n- Derive the smallest reliable change that satisfies the outcome conditions and established invariant while preserving\\n  required constraints.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\n### Outcome and Invariant Derivation\\n\\nBefore applying this rule, lazy load `../../common/intermediate-vs-terminal-goals.md` for terminal-goal and acceptance\\nevidence guidance.\\n\\nUse backward design and iterative generalization together before recommending or designing a change; neither is complete\\nwithout the other. Apply the method before adopting, extending, or editing the proposal.\\n\\n### Iterative Generalization and Scope\\n\\nTreat Iterative Generalization as a design gate, not a label for an already chosen solution. When\\nthe available cases or evidence do not prove that a broader, merged, or shorter statement preserves every existing\\nreader decision, retain the narrower existing statement and report the candidate improvement; do not infer that similar\\nwording permits a generalization.\\n\\nBefore adding a normative rule paragraph, make the generalization evidence explicit: identify the concrete case, one\\nmeaningful analogous case, one relevant dissimilar case, and the invariant that survives all three. Decide explicitly whether the shared invariant\\nbelongs in a broader rule or must remain narrow, and retain the reason as part of the design checkpoint.\\n# Class Design\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Make each component's responsibility, lifecycle, ownership, safety, and concurrency guarantees explicit, and keep its\\n  API and collaboration boundaries compatible with them.\\n- Make components replaceable and testable only where a supported variation or external integration needs a boundary,\\n  without exposing unsafe convenience paths, test-only production responsibilities, or trivial indirection.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nWhen designing or changing a component, API, collaborator, variation point, integration boundary, construction path, or\\ntest-support boundary, first identify the guarantees each participant needs: caller-visible results and failures,\\nownership and lifecycle, safety, concurrency, and the supported variations. Evaluate only the conditions that can\\nprevent those guarantees: one component owns unrelated outcomes; a supported variant requires changing stable policy;\\nan implementation weakens a contract; a consumer receives operations it does not need; or policy depends directly on\\nintegration mechanics. Restore a failed guarantee with the smallest boundary or contract that makes it verifiable. Do\\nnot add an abstraction when no independent variation, external integration, or testable boundary needs one.\\n\\nWhen supported variants differ in behavior, put that behavior behind a narrow contract and add an implementation rather\\nthan repeatedly extending a central conditional. Every implementation must preserve its contract's caller-visible\\npreconditions, results, state guarantees, and failure behavior. Give each consumer only the operations it uses, and keep\\nhigh-level policy independent of an integration's concrete mechanics. When deciding\\nwhether an explicit Java null check is unnecessary, lazy load `../java/unnecessary-null-checks.md`.\\n# Error Handling\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Preserve precise failure semantics at intentional error boundaries while giving callers the most specific safely\\n  diagnosed cause and actionable recovery guidance.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nUse the most specific practical error type when raising, catching, or declaring failures. Ask for input only when authority,\\npreference, unavailable information, security, or another confirmation requirement prevents autonomous action.\\n# Test-Driven Development\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Preserve a focused behavioral test's contract from its demonstrated failure before production implementation through\\n  the implementation and relevant verification that make it pass.\\n- Make the decision to use TDD explicit before the first production-behavior edit, rather than relying on the task's\\n  label or the agent's implicit classification.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\n## Applicability\\n\\nBefore the first edit to production behavior, classify the proposed edit. When no focused automated check is practical, state the constraint\\nand the alternate boundary evidence before editing production behavior.\\n\\n## Red-Test Gate\\n\\nBefore editing production behavior for a testable outcome, add or update only the focused behavioral test and run its\\nnarrowest command. If a test cannot be\\nwritten first because the behavior exists only at an external boundary, explain the constraint and add the smallest\\nreliable boundary test after implementing the behavior.\\n# Testing Focus and Isolation\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Test observable behavior with isolated, controlled inputs and state, ensuring each claim, exercised boundary, and\\n  assertion describe that same outcome and remain distinct from structural artifact validation.\\n- Ensure an artifact-wide audit finds every executable verification artifact whose claimed outcome is not directly\\n  exercised and observed.\\n- Make application behavior directly and safely testable in the same process by passing environmental dependencies\\n  explicitly when shared process state would otherwise prevent isolation.\\n- Verify meaningful changes efficiently with the narrowest relevant test and the complete suite before handoff.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nTest observable behavior with controlled inputs rather than machine-specific configuration or implementation details.\\nEach test owns its fixtures and mutable state. Avoid tests that primarily validate third-party tools; test the\\napplication's interpretation, command construction, error handling, and integration behavior instead.\\n\\nChoose the test language from the behavior being claimed, not from the fact that it uses a command, files, or another\\ntool. Run the narrowest relevant test after a meaningful\\nchange, then the complete verification suite before handoff.\\n\\nBefore accepting any test, state in one plain sentence what it says happens and identify the operation that makes it\\nhappen. Correct every unsupported claim by narrowing it, adding the missing\\ndirect exercise and assertion, or splitting independently observable outcomes.\\n\\nStructural artifact tests are allowed when their claim is limited to packaged layout or validity. A dependency that adds more contract, risk, or\\nmaintenance than that local behavior is not a suitable option.\\n# Constants\\n\\n## Design Goals\\n\\n- Centralize repeated constants behind meaningful names and one authoritative definition.\\n- Keep maintained resource-layout and protocol identifiers authoritative even before more than one consumer uses them.\\n- Keep constants in a readable, semantically meaningful form until an interface requires a different\\n  representation.\\n\\n## Guidance\\n\\nWhen the same meaningful value is inlined in multiple semantically coupled places, define it once as a clearly named\\nconstant at the narrowest common layer that owns its meaning, then reference it everywhere it applies.\\n\\nTreat a formatted, encoded, or otherwise derived representation as another use of its source value. Name every decision the feature must make, the authoritative source that\\nestablishes the correct answer, the actor authorized to provide or change that source, and the validation that can\\ndistinguish a correct result from a plausible one.\\n\\nApply the **information-sufficiency test** to each decision. This is a proof of a missing input, not a request to improve the inference.\\n\\nTreat the following as warning signals that require this test:\\n\\n- The feature must classify intent, support status, business meaning, ownership, priority, feature boundaries, or\\n  another subjective/specification decision, but its allowed inputs are only code, history, or generated artifacts.\\n- The feature claims to work for arbitrary user projects while the required decision depends on project-specific\\n  contracts, audiences, workflows, or terminology that no supplied specification defines.\\n- The feature must prove its own inferred label, mapping, or grouping correct, but no independent oracle, regression,\\n  authoritative contract, or user approval can reject a wrong result.\\n- The feature must compare identities or equivalence classes but no canonical representation or approved mapping exists.\\n- The requested guarantee excludes the only actor or authority that can supply the needed decision.\\n- The proposed acceptance check can show that the feature ran, but cannot distinguish a correct result from a convincing\\n  incorrect one.\\n\\nDo not issue a feasibility warning merely because work is difficult, slow, novel, or unimplemented. +package checkout
+
+import "testing"
+
+func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculate(t *testing.T) {
+	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name         string
+		itemPrice    string
+		discountRate string
+		taxRate      string
+		shipping     ShippingMethod
+		want         string
+	}{
+		{
+			name:         "standard shipping applies discount before tax",
+			itemPrice:    "100.00",
+			discountRate: "0.10",
+			taxRate:      "0.05",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "94.50",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "expedited shipping is added before tax",
+			itemPrice:    "100.00",
+			discountRate: "0.10",
+			taxRate:      "0.05",
+			shipping:     ExpeditedShipping,
+			want:         "110.25",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "rounds exact halfway values to even cents",
+			itemPrice:    "0.005",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "0.00",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "rounds an odd halfway cent upward",
+			itemPrice:    "0.015",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "0.02",
+		},
+	}
+
+	for _, test := range tests {
+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			got, err := calculator.Calculate(
+				test.itemPrice,
+				test.discountRate,
+				test.taxRate,
+				test.shipping,
+			)
+			if err != nil {
+				t.Fatalf("Calculate() returned an error: %v", err)
+			}
+			if got != test.want {
+				t.Errorf("Calculate() = %q, want %q", got, test.want)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculateRejectsInvalidInput(t *testing.T) {
+	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name         string
+		itemPrice    string
+		discountRate string
+		taxRate      string
+		shipping     ShippingMethod
+	}{
+		{
+			name:         "price is not a plain decimal",
+			itemPrice:    "1e2",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "discount exceeds one",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "1.01",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "tax exceeds one",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "1.01",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "shipping method is unsupported",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     ShippingMethod("overnight"),
+		},
+	}
+
+	for _, test := range tests {
+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			_, err := calculator.Calculate(
+				test.itemPrice,
+				test.discountRate,
+				test.taxRate,
+				test.shipping,
+			)
+			if err == nil {
+				t.Fatal("Calculate() returned nil error")
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}

package checkout

import (
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
	"strings"
)

const (
	expeditedShippingFee = 15
	centsPerUnit         = 100
)

// ShippingMethod is the delivery option selected for a checkout.
type ShippingMethod string

const (
	// StandardShipping adds no shipping fee.
	StandardShipping ShippingMethod = "standard"
	// ExpeditedShipping adds a 15.00 fee before tax is calculated.
	ExpeditedShipping ShippingMethod = "expedited"
)

var one = big.NewRat(1, 1)

// CheckoutPriceCalculator calculates a checkout total for one item.
type CheckoutPriceCalculator struct {
}

// Calculate returns the checkout total in one currency with exactly two decimal
// places. Inputs must use plain nonnegative decimal notation. Discount and tax
// rates are decimal fractions from zero through one, inclusive.
func (CheckoutPriceCalculator) Calculate(
	itemPrice string,
	discountRate string,
	taxRate string,
	shipping ShippingMethod,
) (string, error) {
	if shipping != StandardShipping && shipping != ExpeditedShipping {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("shipping method %q is invalid; use %q or %q", shipping, StandardShipping, ExpeditedShipping)
	}

	price, err := parsePlainDecimal("item price", itemPrice)
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	discount, err := parseRate("discount rate", discountRate)
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	tax, err := parseRate("tax rate", taxRate)
	if err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	discountedPrice := new(big.Rat).Mul(price, new(big.Rat).Sub(one, discount))
	subtotal := new(big.Rat).Set(discountedPrice)
	if shipping == ExpeditedShipping {
		subtotal.Add(subtotal, big.NewRat(expeditedShippingFee, 1))
	}

	total := new(big.Rat).Mul(subtotal, new(big.Rat).Add(one, tax))
	return formatRoundedToCents(total), nil
}

func parseRate(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
	rate, err := parsePlainDecimal(name, value)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if rate.Cmp(one) > 0 {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is outside the allowed range [0, 1]", name, value)
	}

	return rate, nil
}

func parsePlainDecimal(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
	if !isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value) {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is invalid; use digits with an optional decimal point", name, value)
	}

	coefficientText := strings.ReplaceAll(value, ".", "")
	coefficient, ok := new(big.Int).SetString(coefficientText, 10)
	if !ok {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q cannot be parsed", name, value)
	}

	decimalPlaces := len(value) - strings.Index(value, ".") - 1
	if !strings.Contains(value, ".") {
		decimalPlaces = 0
	}

	denominator := new(big.Int).Exp(big.NewInt(10), big.NewInt(int64(decimalPlaces)), nil)
	return new(big.Rat).SetFrac(coefficient, denominator), nil
}

func isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value string) bool {
	if value == "" {
		return false
	}

	digitsAfterDecimalPoint := 0
	for _, character := range value {
		switch {
		case character >= '0' && character <= '9':
			if digitsAfterDecimalPoint > 0 {
				digitsAfterDecimalPoint++
			}
		case character == '.' && digitsAfterDecimalPoint == 0:
			digitsAfterDecimalPoint = 1
		default:
			return false
		}
	}

	return value[0] != '.' && value[len(value)-1] != '.'
}

func formatRoundedToCents(amount *big.Rat) string {
	numerator := new(big.Int).Mul(amount.Num(), big.NewInt(centsPerUnit))
	denominator := amount.Denom()
	cents := new(big.Int)
	remainder := new(big.Int)
	cents.QuoRem(numerator, denominator, remainder)

	doubledRemainder := new(big.Int).Lsh(remainder, 1)
	if doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) > 0 || (doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) == 0 && cents.Bit(0) == 1) {
		cents.Add(cents, big.NewInt(1))
	}

	centsText := cents.String()
	if len(centsText) < 3 {
		centsText = strings.Repeat("0", 3-len(centsText)) + centsText
	}

	return centsText[:len(centsText)-2] + "." + centsText[len(centsText)-2:]
}
package checkout

import "testing"

func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculate(t *testing.T) {
	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}

	tests := []struct {
		name         string
		itemPrice    string
		discountRate string
		taxRate      string
		shipping     ShippingMethod
		want         string
	}{
		{
			name:         "standard shipping applies discount before tax",
			itemPrice:    "100.00",
			discountRate: "0.10",
			taxRate:      "0.05",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
			want:         "94.50",
		},
		{
			name:         "expedited shipping is added before tax",
			itemPrice:    "100.00",
			discountRate: "0.10",
			taxRate:      "0.05",
			shipping:     ExpeditedShipping,
			want:         "110.25",
		},
		{
			name:         "rounds exact halfway values to even cents",
			itemPrice:    "0.005",
			discountRate: "0",
			taxRate:      "0",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
			want:         "0.00",
		},
		{
			name:         "rounds an odd halfway cent upward",
			itemPrice:    "0.015",
			discountRate: "0",
			taxRate:      "0",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
			want:         "0.02",
		},
	}

	for _, test := range tests {
		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			got, err := calculator.Calculate(
				test.itemPrice,
				test.discountRate,
				test.taxRate,
				test.shipping,
			)
			if err != nil {
				t.Fatalf("Calculate() returned an error: %v", err)
			}
			if got != test.want {
				t.Errorf("Calculate() = %q, want %q", got, test.want)
			}
		})
	}
}

func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculateRejectsInvalidInput(t *testing.T) {
	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}

	tests := []struct {
		name         string
		itemPrice    string
		discountRate string
		taxRate      string
		shipping     ShippingMethod
	}{
		{
			name:         "price is not a plain decimal",
			itemPrice:    "1e2",
			discountRate: "0",
			taxRate:      "0",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
		},
		{
			name:         "discount exceeds one",
			itemPrice:    "1",
			discountRate: "1.01",
			taxRate:      "0",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
		},
		{
			name:         "tax exceeds one",
			itemPrice:    "1",
			discountRate: "0",
			taxRate:      "1.01",
			shipping:     StandardShipping,
		},
		{
			name:         "shipping method is unsupported",
			itemPrice:    "1",
			discountRate: "0",
			taxRate:      "0",
			shipping:     ShippingMethod("overnight"),
		},
	}

	for _, test := range tests {
		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			_, err := calculator.Calculate(
				test.itemPrice,
				test.discountRate,
				test.taxRate,
				test.shipping,
			)
			if err == nil {
				t.Fatal("Calculate() returned nil error")
			}
		})
	}
}

+type CheckoutPriceCalculator struct{}

+func (CheckoutPriceCalculator) Calculate(
+	itemPrice string,
+	discountRate string,
+	taxRate string,
+	shipping ShippingMethod,
+) (string, error) {
+	if shipping != StandardShipping && shipping != ExpeditedShipping {

+	}
+
+	price, err := parsePlainDecimal("item price", itemPrice)

+		return "", err

+
+	discount, err := parseRate("discount rate", discountRate)
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+

+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+

+	subtotal := new(big.Rat).Set(discountedPrice)

+	}
+

+	return formatRoundedToCents(total), nil

+func parseRate(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
+	rate, err := parsePlainDecimal(name, value)
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, err
+	}
+	if rate.Cmp(one) > 0 {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is outside the allowed range [0, 1]", name, value)
+	}
+
+	return rate, nil
+}

+func parsePlainDecimal(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
+	if !isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value) {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is invalid; use digits with an optional decimal point", name, value)
+	}
+
+	coefficientText := strings.ReplaceAll(value, ".", "")
+	coefficient, ok := new(big.Int).SetString(coefficientText, 10)
+	if !ok {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q cannot be parsed", name, value)
+	}
+
+	decimalPointIndex := strings.Index(value, ".")
+	decimalPlaces := 0
+	if decimalPointIndex >= 0 {
+		decimalPlaces = len(value) - decimalPointIndex - 1
+	}
+
+	denominator := new(big.Int).Exp(big.NewInt(10), big.NewInt(int64(decimalPlaces)), nil)
+	return new(big.Rat).SetFrac(coefficient, denominator), nil

+
+func isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value string) bool {
+	if value == "" {
+		return false
+	}
+

+	for _, character := range value {
+		switch {
+		case character >= '0' && character <= '9':
+		case character == '.' && !decimalPointSeen:
+			decimalPointSeen = true
+		default:
+			return false
+		}
+	}
+
+	return value[0] != '.' && value[len(value)-1] != '.'
+}

+func formatRoundedToCents(amount *big.Rat) string {
+	numerator := new(big.Int).Mul(amount.Num(), big.NewInt(centsPerUnit))
+	denominator := amount.Denom()
+	cents := new(big.Int)
+	remainder := new(big.Int)

+

+	if doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) > 0 || (doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) == 0 && cents.Bit(0) == 1) {
+		cents.Add(cents, big.NewInt(1))
+	}
+
+	centsText := cents.String()
+	if len(centsText) < 3 {
+		centsText = strings.Repeat("0", 3-len(centsText)) + centsText
+	}
+
+	return centsText[:len(centsText)-2] + "." + centsText[len(centsText)-2:]
 }

+// ShippingMethod is the delivery option selected for a checkout.
+type ShippingMethod string
+
+const (
+	// StandardShipping adds no shipping fee.
+	StandardShipping ShippingMethod = "standard"
+	// ExpeditedShipping adds a 15.00 fee before tax is calculated.
+	ExpeditedShipping ShippingMethod = "expedited"
+)
+
+var one = big.NewRat(1, 1)
+
+// CheckoutPriceCalculator calculates a checkout total for one item.
+type CheckoutPriceCalculator struct{}
+
+// Calculate returns the checkout total in one currency with exactly two decimal
+// places. Inputs must use plain nonnegative decimal notation. Discount and tax
+// rates are decimal fractions from zero through one, inclusive.
+func (CheckoutPriceCalculator) Calculate(
+	itemPrice string,
+	discountRate string,
+	taxRate string,
+	shipping ShippingMethod,
+) (string, error) {
+	if shipping != StandardShipping && shipping != ExpeditedShipping {
+		return "", fmt.Errorf("shipping method %q is invalid; use %q or %q", shipping, StandardShipping, ExpeditedShipping)
+	}
+
+	price, err := parsePlainDecimal("item price", itemPrice)
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+
+	discount, err := parseRate("discount rate", discountRate)
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+
+	tax, err := parseRate("tax rate", taxRate)
+	if err != nil {
+		return "", err
+	}
+
+	discountedPrice := new(big.Rat).Mul(price, new(big.Rat).Sub(one, discount))
+	subtotal := new(big.Rat).Set(discountedPrice)
+	if shipping == ExpeditedShipping {
+		subtotal.Add(subtotal, big.NewRat(expeditedShippingFeeCents, centsPerUnit))
+	}
+
+	total := new(big.Rat).Mul(subtotal, new(big.Rat).Add(one, tax))
+	return formatRoundedToCents(total), nil
+}
+
+func parseRate(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
+	rate, err := parsePlainDecimal(name, value)
+	if err != nil {
+		return nil, err
+	}
+	if rate.Cmp(one) > 0 {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is outside the allowed range [0, 1]", name, value)
+	}
+
+	return rate, nil
+}
+
+func parsePlainDecimal(name string, value string) (*big.Rat, error) {
+	if !isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value) {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q is invalid; use digits with an optional decimal point", name, value)
+	}
+
+	coefficientText := strings.ReplaceAll(value, ".", "")
+	coefficient, ok := new(big.Int).SetString(coefficientText, 10)
+	if !ok {
+		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s %q cannot be parsed", name, value)
+	}
+
+	decimalPointIndex := strings.Index(value, ".")
+	decimalPlaces := 0
+	if decimalPointIndex >= 0 {
+		decimalPlaces = len(value) - decimalPointIndex - 1
+	}
+
+	denominator := new(big.Int).Exp(big.NewInt(10), big.NewInt(int64(decimalPlaces)), nil)
+	return new(big.Rat).SetFrac(coefficient, denominator), nil
+}
+
+func isPlainNonnegativeDecimal(value string) bool {
+	if value == "" {
+		return false
+	}
+
+	decimalPointSeen := false
+	for _, character := range value {
+		switch {
+		case character >= '0' && character <= '9':
+		case character == '.' && !decimalPointSeen:
+			decimalPointSeen = true
+		default:
+			return false
+		}
+	}
+
+	return value[0] != '.' && value[len(value)-1] != '.'
+}
+
+func formatRoundedToCents(amount *big.Rat) string {
+	numerator := new(big.Int).Mul(amount.Num(), big.NewInt(centsPerUnit))
+	denominator := amount.Denom()
+	cents := new(big.Int)
+	remainder := new(big.Int)
+	cents.QuoRem(numerator, denominator, remainder)
+
+	doubledRemainder := new(big.Int).Lsh(remainder, 1)
+	if doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) > 0 || (doubledRemainder.Cmp(denominator) == 0 && cents.Bit(0) == 1) {
+		cents.Add(cents, big.NewInt(1))
+	}
+
+	centsText := cents.String()
+	if len(centsText) < 3 {
+		centsText = strings.Repeat("0", 3-len(centsText)) + centsText
+	}
+
+	return centsText[:len(centsText)-2] + "." + centsText[len(centsText)-2:]
 }

+package checkout
+
+import "testing"
+
+func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculate(t *testing.T) {
+	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name         string
+		itemPrice    string
+		discountRate string
+		taxRate      string
+		shipping     ShippingMethod
+		want         string
+	}{
+		{
+			name:         "standard shipping applies discount before tax",
+			itemPrice:    "100.00",
+			discountRate: "0.10",
+			taxRate:      "0.05",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "94.50",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "expedited shipping is added before tax",
+			itemPrice:    "100.00",
+			discountRate: "0.10",
+			taxRate:      "0.05",
+			shipping:     ExpeditedShipping,
+			want:         "110.25",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "rounds exact halfway values to even cents",
+			itemPrice:    "0.005",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "0.00",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "rounds an odd halfway cent upward",
+			itemPrice:    "0.015",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "0.02",
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "preserves precision beyond binary floating point",
+			itemPrice:    "9007199254740993.015",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+			want:         "9007199254740993.02",
+		},
+	}
+
+	for _, test := range tests {
+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			got, err := calculator.Calculate(
+				test.itemPrice,
+				test.discountRate,
+				test.taxRate,
+				test.shipping,
+			)
+			if err != nil {
+				t.Fatalf("Calculate() returned an error: %v", err)
+			}
+			if got != test.want {
+				t.Errorf("Calculate() = %q, want %q", got, test.want)
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}
+
+func TestCheckoutPriceCalculatorCalculateRejectsInvalidInput(t *testing.T) {
+	calculator := CheckoutPriceCalculator{}
+
+	tests := []struct {
+		name         string
+		itemPrice    string
+		discountRate string
+		taxRate      string
+		shipping     ShippingMethod
+	}{
+		{
+			name:         "price is not a plain decimal",
+			itemPrice:    "1e2",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "discount exceeds one",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "1.01",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "tax exceeds one",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "1.01",
+			shipping:     StandardShipping,
+		},
+		{
+			name:         "shipping method is unsupported",
+			itemPrice:    "1",
+			discountRate: "0",
+			taxRate:      "0",
+			shipping:     ShippingMethod("overnight"),
+		},
+	}
+
+	for _, test := range tests {
+		t.Run(test.name, func(t *testing.T) {
+			_, err := calculator.Calculate(
+				test.itemPrice,
+				test.discountRate,
+				test.taxRate,
+				test.shipping,
+			)
+			if err == nil {
+				t.Fatal("Calculate() returned nil error")
+			}
+		})
+	}
+}
